title: "Why Kerala's crackdown on unregulated cosmetics and supplements matter"
author: "Abey Sushan"

description: "Closing regulatory loopholes will prevent mercury induced kidney disease in hundreds of unsuspecting teenagers"

In a hospital ward, medicine begins with the patient in front of you. Recently, in Malappuram, that patient was a 17-year-old girl who developed severe swelling and heavy protein loss in her urine. The clinical diagnosis was secondary membranous nephropathy—a serious kidney disorder in which the organ’s delicate filtering membranes are damaged by immune complexes.
The trigger was not an infection or an autoimmune flare. It was a jar of fairness cream bought online after being promoted on Instagram. When an accredited laboratory analysed the cream, it was found to contain 1.25 per cent mercury—12,500 parts per million. India’s Cosmetics Rules permit no more than 1 ppm as an unavoidable trace impurity. She had been applying a neurotoxic, nephrotoxic heavy metal to her skin at 12,500 times the legal limit.
Cases like hers—and similar accounts now surfacing publicly from other users—expose a familiar public health problem: clinical teams are left treating preventable organ damage because regulation stopped where modern commerce begins.
Following the Malappuram case, the Kerala Health Department’s move to frame strict guidelines—mandating formal licensing and registration for all offline and online cosmetics and protein supplements. Treating a 17-year-old with mercury-induced kidney disease and helping her recover is good clinical medicine. Closing the regulatory loopholes so the next five hundred teenagers never apply 12,500 ppm of mercury to their skin is public health.
